Making the retrieval layer inspectable

A document chatbot can produce a fluent answer while hiding an important question: did it actually retrieve the right source? Evidence Lab separates the steps so a visitor can inspect the evidence before trusting generated text.

The project brings together document ingestion, chunking, lexical and semantic retrieval, optional local LLM inference, source citations and evaluation in a working application. Simple mode chooses defaults for someone who just wants to upload a file and ask a question. Advanced mode exposes the retrieval strategy, embedding model, answer model, chunk size and retrieval depth.

It is a practical AI engineering portfolio project: the interface, state management, worker lifecycle and failure handling matter alongside the retrieval algorithm.

A RAG pipeline that runs in the browser

Upload documents→Extract text / OCR→Chunk & index→Retrieve evidence→Inspect sources / generate answer

Ingest documents with source provenance

PDF.js extracts text from PDFs and retains page numbers. UTF-8 text and Markdown can be indexed directly. Tesseract performs English OCR for supported images and PDF pages without selectable text. OCR provenance stays attached to the extracted material, because recognition errors should remain visible when inspecting a source.

Text becomes overlapping word windows. The visitor can choose 60, 120 or 240 words per chunk in Advanced mode. PDF chunks stay within their source page, so a retrieved passage can point back to a specific page instead of an ambiguous whole document.

Separate interface and model work

The application uses JavaScript and Web Workers to handle embedding and answer-model operations separately from the interface. Workers report their progress to a visible operation card. Cancellation, timeouts and stale-worker checks help the interface recover when a download fails or the user stops an operation.

GitHub Pages serves the static application for free. There is no application backend or server-side document database. Documents and derived vectors remain in session memory; model files may be cached by the browser. Initial model and runtime downloads contact their hosting providers, and the page loads fonts from Google Fonts.

BM25, semantic search and hybrid retrieval

BM25 provides fast lexical retrieval without downloading model weights. It is useful when the question and document share exact terms, identifiers or error codes. Semantic retrieval uses quantized MiniLM or BGE Small English embeddings, allowing related wording to match even when the same words do not appear in both the query and passage.

Hybrid modes combine BM25 with either embedding model through reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). RRF combines rank positions instead of adding incomparable raw scores. The pipeline retrieves up to 20 candidates per strategy, removes duplicate passages and returns the selected number of final evidence passages.

Every result exposes its source and chunk location. A downloadable JSON query trace records the effective configuration and retrieval results, making a particular answer easier to inspect and reproduce.

Model choice is a tradeoff. MiniLM has a smaller weight download; BGE has a longer supported input window. Embedding inputs still have token limits, and cosine-similarity thresholds are heuristics rather than confidence scores.

Optional local LLM answers with WebLLM

The evidence-only path displays retrieved excerpts without generating an answer. Optional WebLLM generation uses the visitor’s GPU to turn the retrieved context into a response. Available choices include SmolLM2 135M, Qwen2.5 0.5B and 1.5B, and Llama 3.2 3B. Weight downloads range from about 269 MB to 1.81 GB, with additional runtime files and GPU memory requirements.

Simple mode automatically attempts hybrid BM25 + MiniLM retrieval and Qwen2.5 0.5B generation. Advanced mode starts with BM25 and evidence-only answers, leaving model selection to the visitor. If local generation cannot run, the retrieved source excerpts remain useful.

The generation prompt contains numbered source passages and a bounded context. A citation check detects missing or invalid source references. When that check fails, the interface replaces the model output with original source excerpts. Valid citation numbers alone do not prove that an answer is factually supported.

What the retrieval evaluation measured

The built-in comparison uses eight synthetic documents, twelve answerable questions and three unanswerable questions. One question requires two relevant sources. All methods are evaluated at a retrieval depth of three.

The following numbers are from a saved browser run on 15 October 2026. The live comparison computes a fresh run; it does not populate the interface from these saved results.

Observed engineering-v1 retrieval results on a small authored dataset
MethodHit@1Recall@3MRR@3False evidence
BM2566.7%66.7%0.66733.3%
MiniLM100.0%95.8%1.0000.0%
BGE Small91.7%95.8%0.95833.3%
Hybrid BM25 + BGE91.7%100.0%0.95833.3%

Hit@1 asks whether the first result is a labeled source. Recall@3 measures how many labeled sources appear in the top three. MRR@3 rewards an earlier first relevant result. False evidence counts whether the system returns any evidence for an unanswerable question.

These results do not establish a universal best model. The dataset is authored and small, not held out. A 33.3% false-evidence rate here means one of only three questions; it is not a generated-answer hallucination rate.

Inspect the evaluation methodology and complete saved rankings and labels. A stronger production evaluation would use representative documents, independently labeled questions and a larger set of no-answer cases.

Practical limits and engineering decisions

  • Bound the workload. Uploads are limited to 2 MiB per file, 20 documents and 8 MiB of extracted text per session. Semantic retrieval supports up to 200 chunks. These limits help avoid exhausting browser memory.
  • Keep a useful fallback. BM25 does not require a model download. Source excerpts remain available if WebGPU or local generation fails.
  • Make uncertainty visible. OCR can misread text, PDF reading order can be imperfect, and retrieved passages can be irrelevant. Similarity scores and citation numbers do not establish truth.
  • Be precise about privacy. The app does not send document contents or questions to an application service. Hosting and model providers still receive normal resource-download requests. Browser caches and session memory are not a persistent document workspace.
  • Distinguish a demo from production infrastructure. This project demonstrates browser-local RAG. It does not provide server-side authentication, multi-user storage, an enterprise document permission system or guarantees against prompt injection.

The source repository includes automated PDF, OCR, retrieval, prompt, worker and application-state tests. The audit report describes the defects fixed, browser checks performed and the remaining verification boundaries.

Try the document Q&A workflow

  1. Open Evidence Lab and upload a short text PDF, text file or supported image—or load the sample documents.
  2. Ask a question whose answer appears in the document. Inspect the retrieved excerpts and their source locations.
  3. Switch to Advanced to compare BM25, semantic search or hybrid retrieval. Load an optional answer model if your browser supports WebGPU.
  4. Ask an unsupported question and inspect what the system returns. Download the query trace to see the effective settings and evidence.
